title: Araby
focus: a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion

teacherSummary.text: A boy on North Richmond Street, Dublin, is infatuated with his friend Mangan's sister. When she mentions the Araby bazaar, he promises to bring her a gift. His uncle comes home late and drunk, and the boy reaches the bazaar as it closes. Seeing a shop girl flirt idly, he feels himself 'a creature driven and derided by vanity.'

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Araby,” how does Joyce show a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the imagery you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Araby, how does Joyce develop the idea of a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the imagery in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Araby develops the idea of a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and point of view shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Araby (where it begins, turns and ends) and its imagery shape the reader's understanding of a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Araby suggests about a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's imagery and point of view), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how James Joyce uses imagery in Araby to complicate the reader's understanding of a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Araby within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Araby alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion follows or bends those conventions, using the imagery as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Araby and its treatment of a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's imagery and point of view, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Araby as evidence for a larger claim about a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion in Araby. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Araby as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Araby.

satQuestions.passage: One evening I went into the back drawing-room in which the priest had died. It was a dark rainy evening and there was no sound in the house. Through one of the broken panes I heard the rain impinge upon the earth, the fine incessant needles of water playing in the sodden beds. Some distant lamp or lighted window gleamed below me. I was thankful that I could see so little. All my senses seemed to desire to veil themselves and, feeling that I was about to slip from them, I pressed the palms of my hands together until they trembled, murmuring: "O love! O love!" many times.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Araby”?
options: The cost of wanting to seem richer than you are
A boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion
The futile attempt to shut out death

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Have you ever looked forward to something that disappointed you? Why? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Nothing in this story needs a special warning.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are impinge, converged, derided, garrulous, pitilessly. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “Through one of the broken panes I heard the rain impinge upon the earth, the fine incessant needles of water playing in the sodden beds.” In this sentence it means: to press against or strike upon. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Araby would have known. Collected in Dubliners (1914). The Araby bazaar was a real 1894 Dublin event; Joyce's stories show the 'paralysis' he saw in Irish life. Why does this story matter? A central modernist text for epiphany; in Gale's Short Stories for Students vol. 1. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for imagery.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “One evening I went into the back drawing-room in which the priest had died.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion? I circle “impinge”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find imagery, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for imagery.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of imagery. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Imagery, Point of view, Symbolism: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Araby develops the idea of a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and point of view shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to romantic idealism and disillusionment? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how imagery shapes a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
